title: PCOS Renamed PMOS as Landmark Study Links Condition to Four-Fold Higher Heart Disease Risk
excerpt: A new Lancet study shows women with the condition formerly known as PCOS face quadruple the risk of cardiovascular disease, adding urgency to a global push for better screening and earlier intervention.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Women with PMOS face quadruple the heart disease risk compared to those without, per a Lancet study.
  • PMOS was renamed from PCOS in May 2026 after 14 years of international collaboration.
  • One in five Indian women is affected by PMOS, significantly higher than the global average.
  • The elevated cardiovascular risk persists even when accounting for diabetes and high blood pressure.
  • Women with PMOS (formerly PCOS) face four times the risk of heart disease compared to those without the condition, according to a major Lancet study analysing 413,000 patients.
  • The condition was officially renamed from Polycystic Ovary Syndrome to Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome in May 2026, after 14 years of international collaboration.
  • One in five Indian women is affected, making it one of the most common endocrine disorders in the country.
  • Experts say the elevated cardiovascular risk persists even after accounting for diabetes and high blood pressure.

The Renaming That Changed a Diagnosis

Polycystic Ovary Syndrome, one of the most common hormonal conditions affecting women worldwide, was officially renamed Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) in May 2026. The change, published in The Lancet after 14 years of international collaboration involving 56 organisations and over 22,000 survey responses from clinicians and patients, was driven by a core frustration: the old name focused too narrowly on ovaries and missed the condition's systemic impact.

Now, a new study in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology & Women's Health has delivered the clearest evidence yet of why that broader lens matters. Researchers at the University of Rochester analysed US health insurance data from 2000 to 2022, covering 413,450 women with PMOS aged 18 to 50, matched against more than two million women without the condition.

> **"Women with PMOS showed a four-fold higher risk of cardiovascular disease compared to those without the condition."**

"Women with PMOS showed a four-fold higher risk of cardiovascular disease compared to those without the condition."

Four Times the Heart Disease Risk

The findings are stark. Women with PMOS showed a four-fold higher risk of cardiovascular disease compared to those without the condition. That elevated risk remained even after researchers accounted for the effects of high blood pressure and diabetes — two conditions frequently associated with PMOS.

While heart disease incidence rises with age in all women, the study found it is exacerbated significantly in those with PMOS. The researchers stressed the need for physician education and patient awareness to improve implementation of early preventive measures.

"Our results emphasise the need for physician education and patient awareness of cardiovascular disease risk to improve implementation of early preventive interventions."

— University of Rochester research team, The Lancet

Why the Name Change Matters

The renaming effort, led by organisations including Verity UK, CRE Whirl and AEPCOS, reflects a decade-long push to stop classifying PMOS as primarily a reproductive problem. The condition is characterised by hormonal fluctuations that affect weight, skin, hair growth, mental health and the reproductive system — but its links to Type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, fatty liver disease, endometrial cancer and depression were often overlooked under the old name.

"This condition has multidimensional implications," said Dr Lubna Pal, a reproductive endocrinologist at Yale Medicine who contributed to the renaming effort. "One of the reasons for the switch in terminology is to move away from classifying it as a reproductive disorder."

More than half of affected women report that their symptoms have been dismissed by healthcare professionals, and over a third waited more than four years for a diagnosis, according to the BMJ.

The Indian Connection

The condition affects an estimated one in five women in India, according to The Indian Express — a prevalence rate significantly higher than the global average of one in eight. Indian women in the diaspora face compounded challenges: cultural stigma around hormonal conditions, limited awareness of the metabolic risks, and healthcare systems that may not screen for cardiovascular complications in younger women.

Impact of PMOS Beyond Reproductive Health
›PMOS affects weight, skin, hair growth, and mental health.
›Links to Type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease are significant.
›Over half of women report dismissed symptoms by healthcare professionals.
›More than a third waited over four years for diagnosis.

The UK's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has recommended that women with PMOS be seen by health professionals annually to monitor symptoms and manage long-term risks. The guideline body noted the condition "is frequently underdiagnosed and inconsistently managed."

What Comes Next

The research team behind the renaming plans to spend the next three years helping patients, professionals and governments worldwide transition from PCOS to PMOS. The new name is expected to be included in the 2028 update to the international treatment guideline. For the millions of women affected — particularly in India and across the diaspora — the hope is that a clearer name leads to earlier diagnosis, better screening for heart disease, and treatment that finally matches the full scope of what they are living with.
